items.headline: AI debate has shifted from 'can we' to 'should we', IPG Autumn Conference 2026 hears
items.excerpt: AI dominated the Independent Publishers Guild Autumn Conference, with new IPG research showing adoption among indie publishers has jumped to 76% in 2026 from 42% in 2023, and 72.9% now hold a formal AI policy. The report's blunt finding: AI may have damaged trust between publishers and authors more than it has actually changed workflows.

items.headline: Oxford University Press updates guidelines as AI use 'measurably' under-disclosed
items.excerpt: An OUP survey found a wide gap between how often researchers actually use AI in their writing and how often they declare it, prompting the publisher to rewrite its author submission guidelines. The update pushes disclosure of AI assistance from optional courtesy toward an explicit condition of submission.

items.headline: What Webtoon's New AI Partnership Could Mean for Translators
items.excerpt: Webtoon is rolling out AI auto-translation for self-published Canvas creators plus 'byUS', a Korea-only interactive story-chat service that lets readers generate new stories from existing webcomics. Translators interviewed say the tooling can speed localization but still misses the cultural nuance that East Asian comics depend on.

items.headline: Authors Guild, Co-Plaintiffs Seek Summary Judgment in OpenAI Case
items.excerpt: The Authors Guild and author plaintiffs filed for summary judgment against OpenAI and Microsoft in the consolidated class action over books used to train large language models without license or payment. The filing lands days after the DOJ backed AI firms on fair use in the parallel NYT case.

items.headline: Authors Guild Addresses Anthropic Settlement Concerns
items.excerpt: Claim notices from Anthropic's $1.5bn copyright settlement have left authors and publishers fighting over how each title's award is split. Guild CEO Mary Rasenberger says a reconciliation process should fix allocation errors between rights holders, but metadata gaps are driving much of the confusion.

items.headline: Ask the Chefs: AI and Copyright Licensing
items.excerpt: Four publishing experts respond to the U.S. Department of Justice statement backing OpenAI's fair-use position in the New York Times litigation. The debate turns on whether 'transformative use' can reasonably stretch to cover training a large language model on entire copyrighted corpora.

items.headline: The Unbundling of Scholarly Publishing: A Trilemma for the AI Era
items.excerpt: AI is prying apart the bundle publishers have long held together — corpus, context and community — because each layer can now be discovered and consumed separately through third-party systems. The authors argue publishers must pick which layer they actually defend.

items.headline: A Groupthink We Don't Talk Much About
items.excerpt: The post argues publishing keeps applying AI to the symptoms of runaway research volume rather than the incentives producing it, creating a loop where more volume demands more AI. It names the unspoken consensus that keeps the industry from questioning its own output economics.

items.headline: Writers' AI Fears Often Run Ahead of the Facts
items.excerpt: Friedman takes on three of the loudest writer anxieties — agents secretly using AI, detector false positives, and proving human authorship — and finds the online panic bears little resemblance to agency and publisher practice. She notes rejections tied to detection scores generally start around 20-25%, not at a light AI touch.

items.headline: How Good Are AI Custom-Written Novels?
items.excerpt: A hands-on read of Ember Novels, a service that generates bespoke full-length novels, finds it can hold a plot across roughly 300 pages with noticeably better continuity than earlier AI fiction. The craft ceiling is still low, but the failure mode has moved from incoherence to blandness.

items.headline: Disagreements in the Anthropic Settlement Were Inevitable, But It Feels Worse Than Expected
items.excerpt: Friedman sorts the Anthropic settlement disputes into three categories and pins much of the mess on bad metadata and poor communication from the settlement administrators. Authors and publishers claiming the same titles are discovering nobody agrees on who owns what.

items.headline: What Machines Can't Replace: Why AI Makes Us More Human, With Anna McPhee
items.excerpt: Software engineer and author Anna McPhee describes writing every word herself while running AI hard on research, editing and admin — including custom editing skills permitted only to produce reports, never to touch the text. She argues AI saturation is already driving reader demand for visibly human, imperfect work.

items.headline: Simon & Schuster is making indie publishing easier
items.excerpt: Simon & Schuster relaunched Pocket Books for print deals and added Simon Stream with 50% net e-book royalties, aimed at self-published authors who want a major imprint's stamp. The pitch is explicitly positioned as a way for real books to stand out from the flood of AI-generated slop.

items.headline: NYU Announces Topics and Speakers for 2027 Advanced Publishing Institute
items.excerpt: NYU's January 2027 Advanced Publishing Institute centers on 'Innovation, Audience, and Analytics', with a dedicated session on how publishers are successfully leveraging AI and the controversies that come with it. Speakers include Simon & Schuster CEO Greg Greeley and Stable Book Group's Keith Reigert.
